568.title: Six leaks
568.hook: wealth drains through drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness
568.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often teach the Sigalovada's six leaks to lay people as practical household advice, and Buddhist economics writers cite it alongside the sutta's advice on saving and sharing wealth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: desire, hate, delusion and fear, and your line, four motives. Which one did you catch leaning on a choice? Today, the Buddha talks to Sigala about money. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Open a banking app and look at last month. There's usually no single disaster. Just a lot of small drips: a subscription you forgot, takeout three nights running, a late-night purchase you can't quite remember making. The money didn't explode. It leaked. The Buddha, talking to a young householder in a world with no apps, names the same thing. Six openings, he calls them, through which a household's wealth drains away. Today: six leaks.
screen: `NO DISASTER, JUST DRIPS.` → `A YOUNG HOUSEHOLDER'S BUDGET.` → `SIX OPENINGS.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is apayamukha, literally a mouth or opening toward loss. Here are the six. Drinking intoxicants. Roaming the streets at the wrong hours. Haunting fairs and shows. Gambling. Keeping bad company. And idleness. Then, for each one, the Buddha lists six dangers, and the details are wonderfully specific. Gambling: the winner makes enemies, the loser mourns what he lost, his money is gone, his word isn't trusted when he speaks in public, his friends look down on him, and nobody wants him to marry into their family. Roaming at night: he leaves himself unprotected, and his family and property too, he's suspected of crimes, and rumors attach to him. And idleness has the best list of all. The idle man doesn't work, saying: it's too cold. It's too hot. It's too late. It's too early. I'm too hungry. I'm too full. Every single reason sounds reasonable. That's what makes it a leak. Notice what the Buddha is doing with Sigala. He isn't giving a sermon against pleasure, and he isn't asking a householder to live like a monk. Elsewhere in the same sutta he tells him to enjoy part of his wealth. He's simply pointing to where it goes when you're not watching. The leaks aren't only money, either. Each one drains time, health, trust and friendships too. And none of them is dramatic. It's one more drink, one more night out, one more too late, too early.
screen: `APAYAMUKHA: OPENINGS TO LOSS.` · `SIX LEAKS, SIX DANGERS EACH.` · `TOO COLD, TOO HOT, TOO LATE.` · `NOT A SERMON AGAINST PLEASURE.` · then, large: `SIX LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look honestly at your own week, without blame. Where does something leak? Money, yes, but also time, energy, attention. Let one leak come to mind, the most ordinary one. Picture the moment it usually happens: the evening, the phone, the excuse. Breathe with it. Then picture plugging it once, just once, this week. The bell holds the time.
Six leaks. In DN 31 the six openings through which wealth drains: drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness. Today's word.
Your line: six leaks. Today, plug one leak once, and when the excuse comes, too hot, too late, too tired, smile at it. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

pairs: too cold, too hot, too late

myth: the Buddha tells Sigala to give up all pleasure
the same sutta tells him to enjoy part of his wealth; the leaks are about where it drains.
each leak in DN 31 comes with six dangers
six openings, each with its own list of six.
among the idle man's excuses is 'I'm too full'
too cold, too hot, too late, too early, too hungry, too full.

fork.setup: it's a hot afternoon and there's work to do. the idle man in the Sigalovada has an answer ready. what is it?
options: I'll do twice as much tomorrow.
fork.reveal: it's too hot, and if it isn't, it's too cold, too late, too early, too hungry or too full.

original.note: Pali apayamukha: apaya, loss or ruin; mukha, mouth or opening. the six leaks of DN 31.

trapdoor: what you thought: wealth is lost in big disasters.
what it means: in DN 31 it drains through six ordinary openings, each with its own six dangers.
what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada's apayamukha list, with sixfold dangers for each, is among the most practical economic passages in the Pali canon.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the six channels for dissipating wealth

569.title: The true friend
569.hook: false friends and true friends, and how to tell them apart
569.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers teach the Sigalovada's eight kinds of friend to young people and families, and the Buddha's wider teaching calls good friendship, kalyanamittata, the whole of the holy life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where wealth drains away, and your line, six leaks. Which leak did you plug? One of them was bad company, and today the Buddha tells Sigala how to spot it. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

Moving day. You've asked around: anyone free Saturday? One friend sends ten heart emojis and a long message about how much they wish they could. One says they'll be there, then asks if you can lend them your car next week. One goes quiet. And one just shows up at eight with coffee and a dolly, and stays until the last box is in. The Sigalovada has a name for every one of them. Today: the true friend.
screen: `ANYONE FREE SATURDAY?` → `HEARTS, FAVORS, SILENCE.` → `ONE SHOWS UP AT EIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells Sigala, there are four who look like friends and aren't. The taker, who gives little and asks a lot, and helps only out of fear or for his own gain. The talker, all words: he's generous about the past and the future, but when you need something now, he points to his bad luck. The flatterer, who agrees with whatever you do, good or bad, praises you to your face, and runs you down behind your back. And the companion in wasting: your partner for drinking, for roaming at night, for shows and for gambling. Then four true friends, each with a fine detail. The helper: he looks after you when you're careless, guards your things, is a refuge when you're afraid, and when there's a job to do, gives you twice what you asked for. The one who's the same in good times and bad: he tells you his secrets, keeps yours, doesn't leave you when things go wrong, and would give his life for you. The one who points the way: he keeps you from wrong, encourages what's good, tells you what you haven't heard, and points out the way to heaven. And the one who cares: he doesn't celebrate your bad luck, he's glad at your good luck, stops others when they speak ill of you, and praises those who speak well of you. Notice how practical this is. Every test is something you can watch for. And notice the mirror in it: the same list tells you what kind of friend to be.
screen: `THE TAKER, THE TALKER, THE FLATTERER.` · `THE HELPER GIVES TWICE.` · `THE SAME IN GOOD AND BAD.` · `THE ONE WHO POINTS THE WAY.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND IN NEED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let one true friend come to mind. Someone who showed up. Picture the moment: what they did, how it felt. Breathe that gratitude in. Then ask, quietly, which of the four true friends you are to someone. The helper? The steady one? The one who points the way? The one who cares? After the bell, if you like, send that friend a message of thanks. The bell holds the time.
The true friend. In DN 31, four false friends and four true ones: the helper, the steady one, the one who points the way, and the one who cares. Today's word.
Your line: the friend in need. Today, thank one true friend for a specific time they showed up, and be that friend for someone else. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

pairs: generous about past and future only
praises to your face, runs you down later

he approves of whatever you do, good or bad.
the true helper gives twice what you asked for

the one who cares stops others from speaking ill of you
and praises those who speak well of you.

fork.setup: you need help now. a friend says how much he'd have helped last month, and how he'll help next year, but today he's unlucky. which kind of friend is he?
fork.reveal: the talker: generous about past and future, empty in the present.

original.note: Pali mitta: friend. a true friend is called suhada, good-hearted.

trapdoor: what you thought: a friend is anyone who's nice to you.
what it means: DN 31 gives eight kinds of friend, four false and four true, each with tests you can watch.
what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada contrasts mitta-patirupaka (counterfeit friends) with suhada mitta (good-hearted friends), four of each with four marks apiece.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), false and true friends

570.title: East and south
570.hook: parents and children, teachers and students: duties both ways
570.howItsDone: In some Buddhist countries children bow to their parents and students to their teachers at festivals such as Thailand's teacher-honoring ceremony, and families make offerings and merit in memory of parents who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four false friends and four true ones, and your line, the friend in need. Who did you thank? Today the Buddha finally turns Sigala back toward the sunrise. Day five hundred seventy.

Honor your father and mother. Respect your elders. Listen to your teacher. Rules like these point one way: from the young to the old. The Sigalovada does something worth noticing. Every time it tells the young man what he owes, it turns around and says what is owed to him. Five duties going one way, five coming back, for parents and for teachers alike. A bow in two directions. Today: east and south.
screen: `FROM THE YOUNG TO THE OLD.` → `FIVE DUTIES EACH WAY.` → `A BOW IN TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: East is the parents, the direction where the day begins. A child, the Buddha says, honors them in five ways, thinking: they supported me, so I'll support them. I'll do the work they need done. I'll keep up the family line. I'll be worthy of what they leave me. And when they've died, I'll make offerings in their memory. And parents, honored like this, show their love in five ways too. They keep their child from what's harmful. They encourage what's good. They have the child trained in a skill. They help arrange a suitable marriage. And at the right time, they hand over the inheritance. South is the teachers. A student honors a teacher by rising to greet them, by waiting on them, by being eager to learn, by small acts of service, and by taking the lesson seriously. And the teacher, in return, trains the student well, makes sure they've really understood, teaches them the whole of the craft, speaks well of them to friends, and keeps them safe wherever they go. Read the lists again and notice the balance. The child's list ends with remembering parents after death; the parents' list ends with letting go of what they own at the right time. The student's list ends with attention; the teacher's ends with protection. Some of the details belong to ancient India, arranged marriages and inheritances. But the shape is plain. Respect flows up, and care flows down, and when both flow, the direction is honored.
screen: `EAST: THEY SUPPORTED ME.` · `PARENTS: SKILL, MARRIAGE, INHERITANCE.` · `SOUTH: EAGER TO LEARN.` · `TEACHERS: THE WHOLE CRAFT, AND SAFETY.` · then, large: `EAST AND SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Turn, if you can, toward the east. Bring to mind a parent, or whoever raised you, living or not. Let one thing they gave you come up, and quietly honor it. Then turn toward the south, and bring to mind a teacher: a schoolteacher, a coach, a mentor, someone who showed you how. Let one lesson they gave you come up. If you have children or students yourself, notice the duties coming back the other way. The bell holds the time.
East and south. In DN 31 the east is parents and the south is teachers, each with five duties owed and five returned. Today's word.
Your line: east and south. Today, honor one parent or teacher with a call, a note or a memory, and if you're someone's parent or teacher, do one of your five. Day five hundred seventy.

match.prompt: east and south: tap the pairs.

myth: the Sigalovada lists duties only from children to parents
five duties go each way: parents owe their children too.
one duty of parents is to have their child trained in a skill
along with guarding, encouraging, marriage and inheritance.
a good teacher in DN 31 speaks well of the student to friends
and teaches the whole of the craft.

fork.setup: you're a teacher in the Sigalovada. your student has risen to greet you and is eager to learn. what do you owe back?
options: train them well, teach the whole craft, speak well of them and keep them safe.
fork.reveal: the teacher owes five duties in return, ending with keeping the student safe wherever they go.

original.note: Pali puratthima disa: the eastern direction, which DN 31 gives to parents.

trapdoor: what you thought: honoring parents and teachers is a duty that flows one way.
what it means: DN 31 gives five duties each way, upward and downward.

what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada pairs duties in every direction, five and five (six in return from the renunciants), and Buddhaghosa's commentary calls the whole sutta the householder's discipline (gihi-vinaya).

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the eastern and southern directions

571.title: West, north, below, above
571.hook: spouses, friends, workers, religious teachers: duties both ways
571.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists learn the Sigalovada's duties as a guide to marriage, friendship and work, and households support monastics with food and requisites while monastics teach and counsel in return.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents and teachers, and your line, east and south. Did you honor one of them? Today Sigala turns the rest of the way around, and the bow is complete. Day five hundred seventy-one.

Count the people behind an ordinary day. The person you live with. The friend who texted. The person who made your coffee, or cleaned the office, or delivered the package. Someone whose words you turn to when life gets heavy. Four kinds of people, and it's easy to thank only one or two of them. The last part of the Sigalovada finishes the circle. Four more directions, four more pairs of duties. Today: west.
screen: `THE PEOPLE BEHIND A DAY.` → `EASY TO THANK ONLY ONE OR TWO.` → `THE CIRCLE FINISHED.`

segments.voice: West is the spouse. The husband, in the sutta's world, honors his wife by respecting her, by never looking down on her, by being faithful, by giving her authority in the home, and by giving her gifts. She in return organizes the household well, is kind to both families and to the helpers, is faithful, protects what they've earned, and is skilled and tireless in her work. North is friends. You honor them by giving, by kind words, by helping, by treating them as equals, and by keeping your word. And they, in return, look after you when you're careless, guard your things, are a refuge when you're afraid, don't leave you in trouble, and care about your family too. Below are those who work for you. You give them work suited to their strength, food and wages, care when they're sick, a share of special treats, and time off. And they rise before you, rest after you, take only what's given, do good work, and speak well of you. Above are the spiritual teachers, the monks and brahmins of Sigala's day. You honor them with kindness in deed, word and thought, by keeping your door open to them, and by supplying their needs. They in return keep you from wrong, encourage what's good, care for you with a kind heart, teach you what you haven't heard, clarify what you have, and show you the way to a heavenly rebirth. Some details belong to their own century. Care in sickness and days off for workers still read as fresh. Six directions, and in each one, care going both ways.
screen: `WEST: RESPECT, TRUST, A SHARE OF AUTHORITY.` · `NORTH: KEEP YOUR WORD.` · `BELOW: FAIR WORK, CARE, TIME OFF.` · `ABOVE: AN OPEN DOOR.` · then, large: `EVERY DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and turn your attention to the person who works for you or serves you, whoever it is: someone you employ, a cleaner, a driver, the person at the counter. Picture their face. Let one wish for them come up: good health, fair pay, a rest. Then let the circle widen: west to the person you live with, north to a friend, above to whoever guides you. Every direction, one face each. The bell holds the time.
West. In DN 31 the west is one's spouse; then north for friends, below for workers, above for spiritual teachers, each with duties both ways. Today's word.
Your line: every direction. Today, honor someone who works for you or serves you: thank them by name, or give them a little more time, care or credit. Day five hundred seventy-one.

along with fair work, food and wages, care when sick and a share of treats.
in DN 31 only the wife has duties in a marriage
the husband owes five duties too, including respect and faithfulness.
spiritual teachers owe nothing in return for support
they keep you from wrong, encourage good and teach you what you haven't heard.

fork.setup: you're the head of a household in the Sigalovada. one of your workers falls sick. what does the sutta say you owe?
options: nothing until they come back to work.
fork.reveal: care when sick is one of the five duties toward those who work for you, with fair work, wages, treats and time off.

original.note: Pali pacchima disa: the western direction, which DN 31 gives to one's spouse.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sigalovada is old advice about obeying superiors.
what it means: it gives duties both ways in every relationship, including to workers and from teachers.
what a scholar hears: the treatment of servants and workers (dasa-kammakara) in DN 31, with wages, sick care and leave, is often cited in discussions of Buddhist social ethics.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the western, northern, lower and upper directions

572.title: So it isn't lost
572.hook: a teacher dies, his followers split, and Sariputta answers by counting
572.howItsDone: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions memorize texts and chant them together, and tradition says the Pali discourses were handed down by recitation for centuries before they were written down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: west, north, below, above, and your line, every direction. Did you honor someone who works for you? Today, a new hall, a quarrel next door, and a plan so it doesn't happen again. Day five hundred seventy-two.

In the town of Pava, the local Mallas have just built a new meeting hall, so new that no teacher has used it yet. They invite the Buddha to be the first. He comes with his monks and talks with the townspeople late into the night. When they leave, his back aches. So he asks Sariputta, his senior student, to speak to the monks while he lies down on his right side, mindful. And Sariputta has news from town on his mind. Today: so it isn't lost.
screen: `A NEW HALL IN PAVA.` → `A TEACHER WITH AN ACHING BACK.` → `SARIPUTTA SPEAKS INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Sariputta begins with the news. Nigantha Nataputta, a well-known teacher of the time, the one Jains remember as Mahavira, has recently died here in Pava, and his followers, the discourse says, have split, arguing over what he really taught, wounding each other with words. Then he says, in effect: let's not let that happen to us. Let's recite the teaching together, all of us, in agreement, so that this way of life lasts long, for the good of many. And then he does what you'd do if you wanted a whole room to remember. He counts. One thing: all beings are sustained by food. Two things: name and form. Three things: the roots of harm, greed, hatred and delusion. Four: the foundations of mindfulness. On and on, all the way up to ten. The discourse is called the Sangiti Sutta, the reciting together. Tradition says the teaching was not written down for centuries. It lived in human memory, passed from mouth to ear. A list is a memory tool. A number gives the mind a shelf: if you know there are four, you notice when you've only said three. Some scholars think lists like these were one way the early communities kept a huge body of teaching from drifting. And here's the quiet point. Sariputta's answer to a quarrel isn't a ruling on who was right. It's everyone saying the same words, together, out loud. At the end, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Sariputta, good.
screen: `A TEACHER DIES, A COMMUNITY SPLITS` · `LET'S RECITE IT TOGETHER` · `ONE, TWO, THREE, ALL THE WAY TO TEN` · `SAYING IT TOGETHER KEEPS THE PEACE` · then, large: `SO IT ISN'T LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one list by heart. Pick a short one. The three roots of harm: greed, hatred, delusion. Or the five precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. Sit and settle. Say your list once, slowly, counting it on your fingers. Close your eyes and say it again without looking. Then let the words go and rest on the breath. If it slips away later, that's fine: that's exactly why lists come with numbers. The bell holds the time.
So it isn't lost. Sariputta's reason for reciting the teaching together: so a community stays whole, and the words outlive the people who first heard them. Today's word.
Your line: so it isn't lost. Before bed tonight, count your list on your fingers once more, or teach it to someone at the table. Day five hundred seventy-two.

Sariputta hears that the followers in Pava are quarreling and proposes reciting together.

Sariputta recites them; the Buddha rests and approves at the end.

they climb from ones all the way up to tens.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta. another teacher's followers have split after his death, and the monks are uneasy. what do you do?
options: warn the monks about that other group.
recite the teaching together, number by number.
name a new leader on the spot.
fork.reveal: he proposes a common recitation, so the community agrees on the words and the teaching lasts.

original.note: Pali sangiti: reciting together. the name of DN 33, and later the word for the great councils that recited the canon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long list of numbered teachings is a dry index.
what it means: in DN 33 it's a peace plan: everyone reciting the same words so the community doesn't split.
what a scholar hears: the Sangiti Sutta works like a memory map of the early teaching; some scholars see numbered lists like these as a seed of the later Abhidhamma.

573.title: By tens
573.hook: ten questions asked at every number, from one to ten
573.howItsDone: Many Buddhists learn the teaching through numbered lists, such as the four noble truths, the five precepts and the eightfold path, and monastic study in many countries still includes memorizing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta counting the teaching aloud, and your line, so it isn't lost. Is your list still there? Say it once. Today he counts again, with a twist. Day five hundred seventy-three.

Any good mechanic has a checklist, even if it's only in their head. What's working? What needs attention? What has to come out? What would make this run better? Ask those same few questions of every part, and nothing gets missed. The thirty-fourth discourse, the last of the long ones, is built like that checklist. Sariputta is speaking again, this time beside a lotus pond near the city of Champa. And instead of one list per number, he asks the same ten questions at every number, one through ten. Today: by tens.
screen: `A MECHANIC'S CHECKLIST.` → `BESIDE A LOTUS POND IN CHAMPA.` → `TEN QUESTIONS AT EVERY NUMBER.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the Dasuttara Sutta, roughly, going up to ten. Here's how it works. At number one, Sariputta asks: what one thing helps most? Diligence, care in doing good. What one thing should be developed? Mindfulness of the body, with gladness. What one thing should be fully understood? Contact, the meeting of the senses and the world, the kind that feeds clinging. What one thing should be let go? The conceit I am. What one thing leads to decline? Careless attention. What one thing leads to growth? Wise attention. And so on, ten questions in all, down to: what one thing should be realized? A freedom of mind that can't be shaken. Then he goes to two, and asks all ten questions again, with two things for each answer. Then three. All the way up to ten. Picture a grid: ten numbers down the side, ten questions across the top, and every square filled. It's a whole way of life folded into a table. Notice the questions themselves. They're practical. Not what's true about the universe, but what helps, what to grow, what to drop, what's slipping, what's getting better. You could ask them about a friendship, a job, a morning routine. And notice the pairs, decline and growth. They often turn on the same thing done two ways: careless attention or wise attention. The Long Discourses end here, not with a story or a death scene, but with a teacher handing the community a tool to check itself, number by number.
screen: `TEN QUESTIONS, STARTING AT ONE` · `WHAT HELPS, WHAT TO GROW, WHAT TO DROP` · `THEN ALL TEN AGAIN AT TWO, AND UP` · `A TOOL TO CHECK YOURSELF` · then, large: `BY TENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten good things. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Then, on your fingers, one at a time, name ten good things in your life right now. Small is fine: a warm cup, a friend's message, working knees, a window, a song. One finger for each. Don't rush to ten; let each one land before the next. When your hands are full, rest them in your lap and just breathe with all ten. The bell holds the time.
By tens. Sariputta's last long discourse: ten questions, what helps, what to grow, what to let go, asked again at every number from one to ten. Today's word.
Your line: by tens. Pick one question from today, what helps most, or what should be let go, and ask it once about your own day. Day five hundred seventy-three.

pairs: the one thing that helps most
the one thing to let go

myth: DN 34 is the last discourse in the Long Discourses
the collection of thirty-four ends with Sariputta's ten-by-ten grid.
each number in DN 34 gets only one list
each number gets the same ten questions: what helps, what to develop, what to let go, and more.
the Buddha himself recites DN 34
Sariputta speaks it, beside a lotus pond near Champa.

fork.setup: you're checking on your own life using Sariputta's questions. one thing leads to decline, one to growth. what's the difference?
fork.reveal: at number one, decline comes from careless attention and growth from wise attention: the same mind, used two ways.

original.note: Pali dasuttara: going up to ten. the name of DN 34.

trapdoor: what you thought: by tens means a list of ten things.
what it means: ten questions asked at every number from one to ten, so each square of a grid gets filled.
what a scholar hears: DN 33 and DN 34 close the Digha Nikaya as Sariputta's two great lists; their numbered style is shared with the Anguttara Nikaya and the later Abhidhamma.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 34, Dasuttara Sutta (going up to ten)

574.title: Your long discourse
574.hook: of the long discourses, which one stays with you
574.howItsDone: Individual long discourses, such as the account of the Buddha's last days or the advice to Sigala, are read, chanted and taught on their own in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta's grid, and your line, by tens. Did you count ten good things? Today, the end of a week, and a question only you can answer. Day five hundred seventy-four.

Ask ten people who read the same novel what they remember, and you'll get ten different scenes. One remembers the storm. One remembers a line at a kitchen table. One remembers a side character nobody else noticed. It isn't that nine of them read it wrong. A long book is a house with many rooms, and each reader ends up living in one. For seven weeks, we've walked through the thirty-four Long Discourses. Kings, gods, wanderers, a courtesan, a skeptic prince, a young man bowing to the sky. Today we don't add anything. Today: your long discourse.
screen: `TEN READERS, TEN SCENES.` → `A HOUSE WITH MANY ROOMS.` → `WHICH ROOM DO YOU LIVE IN?`

segments.voice: Some scenes, in case one is waiting for you. A king who killed his own father rides out under a full moon, asking what a spiritual life is good for, and hears that even a slave who goes forth would be honored by a king. A man builds a staircase to a palace he has never seen. A woman named Ambapali invites the Buddha to a meal, and when princes ask for the same day, he keeps his word to her. The Buddha, old and ill, tells Ananda there's no teacher's closed fist: nothing held back. Ananda weeps by a door, and the Buddha praises his long kindness as an attendant. A skeptical prince argues with a monk through story after story. And this week: young Sigala, bowing to six directions, learns what each bow could mean. Six ways wealth leaks away. How to tell a true friend. Duties that run both ways, between parents and children, teachers and students, spouses, friends, workers. Then Sariputta, counting so nothing is lost, and counting again by tens. Here's something the texts themselves suggest. In the last journey, the Buddha says that after he's gone, the teaching and the discipline will be the teacher. Not a person, not a successor: the words. And words do their work by being remembered. That means the scene that stays with you isn't trivia. It's the teacher you actually took home. Yours doesn't have to match anyone else's.
screen: `A MOONLIT KING, A STAIRCASE, A MEAL` · `THIS WEEK: SIGALA'S SIX DIRECTIONS` · `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER` · `THE SCENE THAT STAYED IS YOURS` · then, large: `YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread one scene. Not on a screen; in your mind. Sit and settle. Let one scene from these weeks come up on its own, whichever arrives first. Now walk into it slowly. Where is it? What time of day? Who is speaking? What does the air feel like? Stay inside it for a few breaths, the way you'd stand in a room you love. Then notice why this one came. Don't explain it; just notice. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Your long discourse. The one scene, out of thirty-four discourses, that stayed with you: the teaching you actually carried home. Today's word.
Your line: yours. Tell one person about your scene today, in two sentences, the way you'd tell them about a film. Day five hundred seventy-four.

myth: the Long Discourses are thirty-four discourses
that's the collection we've walked through for seven weeks.
the long discourses are all sermons with no stories
many are stories and conversations: kings, gods, a courtesan, a skeptic prince.
the Buddha names a successor to lead after him
he says the teaching and the discipline will be the teacher.

fork.setup: the Buddha is dying. the monks wonder who will lead them. what does he leave as their teacher?
fork.reveal: in the last journey he says the teaching and discipline he gave will be their teacher after he is gone.

original.note: Pali Digha Nikaya: the long collection, thirty-four discourses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the long discourses are one long book you either know or don't.
what it means: they're thirty-four separate scenes and teachings, and different readers carry different ones home.
what a scholar hears: the Digha Nikaya is grouped in three books, and individual discourses like DN 16 and DN 31 have long histories of being taught and copied on their own.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta: the teaching and discipline as teacher
